title: Odd Even Jump
statement:
You stand at some index of the integer array `arr` and move only forward, by a sequence of jumps numbered 1, 2, 3, ... (the jump's number, not the index, decides its type). From index `i`, the next jump lands on an index `j > i` chosen as follows:

- **Odd-numbered jump** (1st, 3rd, ...): among the later indices with `arr[j] >= arr[i]`, take the one whose value is the smallest.
- **Even-numbered jump** (2nd, 4th, ...): among the later indices with `arr[j] <= arr[i]`, take the one whose value is the largest.
- If several indices share that best value, you must take the leftmost of them. If no later index qualifies, you cannot jump and the walk ends.

A start index is *good* when this walk, beginning with jump 1, reaches the last index `arr.length - 1` (taking zero jumps is allowed, so the last index is always good). Return how many start indices are good.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating the walk from every start costs O(n²) per start in the worst case. Two observations make it fast. First, the target of a jump depends only on the index and the jump's parity, not on the history, so each index has one fixed odd target and one fixed even target. Second, every jump moves right, so whether the end is reachable can be filled in from right to left.

List the indices sorted by value, ties by index. The odd target of `i` is the first index that comes after `i` in that list and also lies to the right of `i` in `arr`. Walking the indices in that sorted order with a monotonic stack of indices finds it: whenever a larger index arrives, it is the answer for every smaller index waiting on top of the stack. Sorting by value descending gives the even targets the same way.

## Approach

1. `nextJump(order)` walks indices in `order`; each arriving `index` pops every waiting index smaller than it and records `index` as their target. The stack stays decreasing from bottom to top.
2. `oddNext` comes from indices sorted by value ascending, `evenNext` from value descending; both break ties by smaller index first.
3. `fromOdd[i]` means "the end is reachable from `i` when the next jump is odd"; `fromEven[i]` likewise for even. Both are true at the last index.
4. Going left, `fromOdd[i] = fromEven[oddNext[i]]` and `fromEven[i] = fromOdd[evenNext[i]]`, staying false when there is no target.
5. Every walk starts with jump 1, so count the indices where `fromOdd[i]` is true.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [10, 13, 12, 14, 15]`. Ascending order is `[0, 2, 1, 3, 4]`, which gives `oddNext = [2, 3, 3, 4, -1]`. Descending order is `[4, 3, 1, 2, 0]`, which gives `evenNext = [-1, 2, -1, -1, -1]`. From the right: `fromOdd[3] = fromEven[4] = true`; `fromOdd[2] = fromEven[3] = false`; `fromOdd[1] = fromEven[3] = false`; `fromOdd[0] = fromEven[2] = false`. Indices 3 and 4 are good, so `good = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the two sorts; each stack pass is O(n) because every index is pushed and popped at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the orders, the stack, the targets and the two tables.

## Pitfalls

- Ties must go to the smaller index in both sorts; sorting the even order by descending index picks the wrong target for repeated values.
- A start index always begins with an odd jump, so count `fromOdd`, not `fromEven`.
- Odd uses `>=` and even uses `<=`: equal values are legal targets for both.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `nextJump` | turns a sorted order of indices into each index's jump target |
| `stack` | indices still waiting for their target, decreasing from bottom to top |
| `oddNext`, `evenNext` | target of an odd or even jump from each index, or `-1` |
| `fromOdd`, `fromEven` | whether the end is reachable when the next jump is odd or even |
| `good` | number of good start indices |
